summary: Describes HyStart++, a modification to the slow start phase of congestion control. It uses a rise in round-trip delay to leave slow start before overshooting, and includes a mitigation so jitter does not trigger a premature exit.

eli5.summary: When filling a bathtub quickly, you slow down as it nears the top rather than overflowing the floor.

questions: how to avoid tcp slow start overshoot
subtitle: A small change to TCP slow start that backs off when delays rise, then checks whether the alarm was false.

tldr.problem: TCP slow start grows the congestion window exponentially and can overshoot the ideal sending rate, causing heavy packet loss that is hard to recover from.
tldr.mechanism: HyStart++ watches the minimum round-trip time of each round and leaves slow start when it rises. It then spends a few rounds in Conservative Slow Start to see whether the rise was just jitter, and resumes slow start if the delay drops back.
tldr.outcome: It reduces packet loss and retransmissions and improves goodput in the lab measurements and deployment data the RFC reports. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9406 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the slow start algorithm in RFC 5681.

sections.title: The Slow Start Overshoot Problem
sections.content:
RFC 5681 describes the slow start algorithm for TCP. It is used while the congestion window (cwnd) is less than the slow start threshold (ssthresh). Without loss signals, TCP grows cwnd exponentially to probe the network capacity.

That fast growth can overshoot the ideal sending rate and cause significant packet loss that cannot always be recovered efficiently. HyStart++ builds on Hybrid Start (HyStart) from the research literature and uses an increase in round-trip delay as a signal to leave slow start before loss happens.

The document describes HyStart++ for TCP, but says it can also be used by other transports that use slow start, such as QUIC (RFC 9002) or SCTP (RFC 9260).
sections.eli5: A new connection speeds up very fast, like a runner sprinting off the line. Sometimes it sprints so fast it crashes into the crowd. HyStart++ helps it slow down in time.

sections.title: The Idea: Exit Early, Then Double-Check
sections.content:
HyStart specifies two algorithms, a Delay Increase algorithm and an Inter-Packet Arrival algorithm. The RFC says the Inter-Packet Arrival algorithm does not perform well in practice, mainly because of ACK compression. HyStart++ keeps only the Delay Increase idea: look for spikes in round-trip time (RTT), which suggest the bottleneck buffer is filling up.

The sender runs standard slow start, and a delay increase triggers an exit. Instead of going straight to congestion avoidance, the sender spends some rounds in Conservative Slow Start (CSS). There the window still grows exponentially, but with a smaller base, so growth is less aggressive.

If the RTT falls during CSS, the earlier spike was not caused by the connection sending too fast, and slow start resumes. If the RTT inflation persists throughout CSS, the connection enters congestion avoidance.
sections.eli5: If the line at the slide gets long, you stop running and walk. If the line shrinks again, you start running. If it stays long, you settle down and wait your turn.

sections.title: The Algorithm Step by Step
sections.content:
Rounds are measured with sequence numbers. windowEnd starts at SND.NXT. When windowEnd is acknowledged, the round ends and windowEnd is set to SND.NXT again. At the start of each round, lastRoundMinRTT takes the old currentRoundMinRTT, and the current minimum and the sample count are reset.

In slow start, each ACK that newly acknowledges N bytes grows the window by min(N, L * SMSS). The sender also tracks the minimum RTT seen in the round. Once at least N_RTT_SAMPLE samples exist, it computes a threshold: RttThresh = max(MIN_RTT_THRESH, min(lastRoundMinRTT / MIN_RTT_DIVISOR, MAX_RTT_THRESH)). If currentRoundMinRTT is at least lastRoundMinRTT + RttThresh, it records cssBaselineMinRtt and enters CSS.

In CSS, the window grows by min(N, L * SMSS) / CSS_GROWTH_DIVISOR per ACK. If a round with enough samples has a currentRoundMinRTT below cssBaselineMinRtt, the exit was spurious and slow start resumes, including HyStart++. CSS lasts at most CSS_ROUNDS rounds, and a partial round at the start counts. When they are done, or if loss or ECN marking is seen at any time, the sender sets ssthresh = cwnd and enters congestion avoidance.
sections.eli5: Each lap, the runner notes the fastest lap time. If this lap's best time is clearly worse than the last one, the track must be crowded, so slow down a bit and watch. If times improve, speed up again. If they stay bad for a few laps, walk.

sections.title: Constants and Tuning
sections.content:
The RFC says it is RECOMMENDED that implementations use the constants in the table below, which were determined with lab measurements and real-world deployments, and that an implementation MAY tune them. Smaller values of MIN_RTT_THRESH may cause spurious slow start exits. Larger values of MAX_RTT_THRESH may mean slow start does not exit until loss on paths with a large RTT.

CSS_GROWTH_DIVISOR MUST be at least 2, because a value of 1 gives the same aggressive behavior as regular slow start. A paced TCP implementation SHOULD use L = infinity. For non-paced implementations, values of L below 8 may suffer slow window growth in high-speed networks, and values above 8 may increase burstiness and loss.

An implementation SHOULD use HyStart++ only for the initial slow start, when ssthresh is still at its arbitrarily high initial value, and fall back to standard slow start afterwards. It MAY also use it to grow the restart window after a long idle period. In application-limited cases a connection might oscillate between CSS and slow start, which the RFC says causes neither premature congestion avoidance nor overshoot.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives a set of recommended settings, like the dials on a game. You can turn them, but turning them too far makes the connection either too jumpy or too slow.

sections.title: Deployment and Measurements
sections.content:
The RFC reports that HyStart++ has been enabled by default for all TCP connections in the Windows operating system for over two years at the time of writing, with pacing disabled and an actual L = 8.

In lab measurements with Windows TCP, it shows better goodput and fewer packet losses and retransmissions than standard slow start. On a 100 Mbps link with a bottleneck buffer of one bandwidth-delay product, bytes retransmitted fell by 50% and retransmission timeouts by 36%.

In an A/B test across a large Windows device population with 52 billion TCP connections, 0.7% of connections moved from 1 RTO to 0 RTOs and another 0.7% moved from 2 RTOs to 1 RTO. The authors note that the test did not focus on send-heavy connections, where they expect the impact to be higher.
sections.eli5: The authors tried it in a lab and on a very large number of real connections. Fewer messages had to be sent again, so things ran smoother.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HyStart++ inherits the security considerations of RFC 5681. An attacker can make it leave slow start too early and hurt a connection's performance, for example by dropping data packets or their acknowledgments.

The ACK division attack from the literature does not affect HyStart++, because window growth is based on the number of bytes newly acknowledged in each ACK rather than a fixed constant per ACK. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker could trick the connection into slowing down too soon by throwing away its messages. But sending lots of tiny fake acknowledgments does not make it speed up unfairly.
